evidence: Ter. Haut. 599: Pessima haec est meretrix.
Ter. Haut. 437: quia pessimē istōc in tē atque in illum cōnsulis
terms.comment: As praise uses the superlative of bonus (see great), blame uses that of malus: “a terrible boy”, puer pessimus. The adverb is pessimē.

evidence: Cic. Att. 14.20.2: L. Antōnī horribilis cōntiō, Dolābellae praeclāra
Catull. 26.5: ō ventum horribilem atque pestilentem!
terms.comment: Properly “frightful” (see terrible, causing fear); in Cicero’s letters and Catullus also the exaggeration of talk: an awful speech, a horrible wind.
Foul, ugly, loathsome; so of weather, a dreadful storm, and morally, shameful (Lewis & Short). A different word from foedus, foederis, a treaty.
Of a journey or an arrangement that went badly (see comfortable).

phrases.latin: Rōmae igitur dē Būthrōtō. L. Antōnī horribilis cōntiō, Dolābellae praeclāra.
phrases.english: So we’ll deal with Buthrotum in Rome. Lucius Antonius made a terrible speech, Dolabella a splendid one.
oh, what a terrible, pestilent wind!

phrases.latin: Actiō māluimus iter facere pedibus quī incommodissimē nāvigāssēmus
phrases.english: after a terrible crossing, we preferred to go on from Actium on foot
